extracted.intended_audience: researchers in NLP/ML working on patent text generation and patent professionals (patent attorneys/agents) interested in automated claim drafting
extracted.subtask_description: Generating patent claims from full patent descriptions (not abstracts) using large language models, and evaluating claim quality with automated metrics and expert human judgments. Focus is on independent and dependent claim sets and model training strategies (fine-tuning, multi-task fine-tuning).

rubrics_metrics.name: BLEU
rubrics_metrics.description: BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy) — a surface-level metric measuring n-gram overlap between generated claims and reference claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a standard automated evaluation metric for text generation; captures word/sequence overlap but not semantic equivalence. Reported in tables comparing abstract-based and description-based generation and across models.

rubrics_metrics.name: ROUGE-1 (R-1)
rubrics_metrics.description: ROUGE-1 — a recall-oriented surface-level metric measuring unigram overlap between generated text and reference text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Captures surface overlap (word-level) and is reported alongside other automated metrics. Useful to quantify lexical coverage of reference claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: ROUGE-L (R-L)
rubrics_metrics.description: ROUGE-L — a surface-level metric based on longest common subsequence (LCS) between the generated and reference texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures sequence-level overlap (captures fluency/ordering agreement); increases reported as evidence of better lexical overlap after fine-tuning.

rubrics_metrics.name: BERTScore
rubrics_metrics.description: BERTScore — a semantic similarity metric using contextual embeddings to score similarity between generated claims and references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantifies semantic similarity beyond surface overlap; used to complement BLEU/ROUGE which are surface-level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of Essential Features
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which the generated claims encapsulate all critical aspects of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human rating scale 0–10 with anchors: 0–2 Most essential features missing; 3–4 Some features present but significant gaps; 5–6 Majority covered with minor omissions; 7–8 Almost all features well described; 9–10 All essential features thoroughly and comprehensively covered. Fine-tuning is noted to improve this criterion. Description-based inputs increase feature completeness compared to abstract-based inputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: The clarity and unambiguity of the language used in the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human rating scale 0–10 with anchors: 0–2 Very unclear/ambiguous; 3–4 Significant clarity issues; 5–6 Mostly clear but some ambiguous language; 7–8 Clear with minimal ambiguity; 9–10 Exceptionally clear and unambiguous. Guidance highlights avoiding ambiguous pronouns (e.g., 'it') and that clarity/precision are paramount for legal enforceability. Multi-task fine-tuning was observed to reduce conceptual clarity in some models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency in Terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformity in the use of terms throughout the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human rating scale 0–10 with anchors: 0–2 Highly inconsistent; 3–4 Significant inconsistencies; 5–6 Some inconsistencies but mostly uniform; 7–8 Largely consistent with minor inconsistencies; 9–10 Completely consistent. Paper notes that even minor inconsistencies can cause rejection or loss of patent value; current LLMs achieve mostly consistent terminology but require perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical Correctness of Feature Linkages
rubrics_metrics.description: The accuracy with which features are interconnected and related within the claim set (i.e., correct logical/technical dependencies between features).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human rating scale 0–10 with anchors: 0–2 Features poorly linked with many inaccuracies; 3–4 Significant linkage issues; 5–6 Mostly accurate with some incorrect connections; 7–8 Accurate with minor inaccuracies; 9–10 Features accurately and correctly linked throughout. Guidance/anti-patterns from paper: avoid randomly selecting features for dependent claims, avoid formulating separate claims that should be summarized into one dependent claim, and ensure grouping of alternative embodiments logically. Fine-tuning improves linkage; GPT-4 groups alternatives logically whereas some models choose features randomly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall Quality (composite score)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregate measure combining completeness, clarity, consistency, and correctness into a single score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Computed as (completeness*4 + clarity*2 + consistency*2 + correctness*3) ÷ 11, producing a 0–10 scale with the same qualitative anchors as other criteria. This weighting emphasizes feature completeness most heavily, then correctness of feature linkage, then clarity and consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate evaluation of first independent claim vs remaining (dependent) claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the first independent claim separately from subsequent dependent claims, as they differ in difficulty and source content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper measures automated metrics and human ratings separately for the first claim and the remaining claims. Observations: first independent claims score significantly higher across metrics (often because descriptions frequently include the independent claim verbatim), whereas remaining dependent claims are much harder and show lower completeness, linkage correctness, and other quality measures. Evaluation protocols should therefore treat these subsets distinctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be crafted with high-level precision and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent claims require strict writing standards, precise and unambiguous wording, and must define the legal protection scope of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims are legally significant and must be precise enough to withstand legal scrutiny. Guidance includes: prefer avoiding pronouns, ensure unambiguous references, and craft claims to be specific enough to distinguish from prior art while broad enough to cover reasonable implementations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent vs Dependent claim structure and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent claims outline essential features broadly; dependent claims incorporate additional features or limitations to refine embodiments and enhance protection scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent claims should aim to encompass the invention broadly while distinguishing from existing technologies. Dependent claims should add meaningful limitations (not mere references) and avoid redundancy. Dependent claims should refine or specify embodiments logically tied to the independent claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pronouns and ambiguous referents
rubrics_metrics.description: References such as 'it' must not introduce ambiguity; preferable to avoid pronouns entirely in claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguous pronouns reduce conceptual clarity and can undermine enforceability. Ensure every referent is explicit and unambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misclassification of feature types (device vs procedural)
rubrics_metrics.description: Features must be classified appropriately (e.g., device-specific features should not be misrepresented as procedural features).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misclassification (e.g., rendering device features as active procedural steps) contradicts standard practice and risks examination objections. Models should preserve the correct grammatical/technical category of features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid repetitive or redundant claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Generated claim sets should not repeatedly restate identical claims or produce multiple claims with no added limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetition signals poor claim drafting and reduces claim set value. Fine-tuning can help reduce repetitions, but models still often generate redundant claims; ensure dependent claims add distinct, substantive limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid null features and non-contributory limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependent claim restrictions should meaningfully contribute to differentiation and protection; features that do not contribute (null features) should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some generated restrictions may not improve protection or differentiation; these should be identified and removed/replaced during revision to improve legal robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology must be completely consistent throughout claim set
rubrics_metrics.description: Domain-specific terminology should be used uniformly across claims to prevent inconsistency-based rejections or loss of clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor inconsistencies can have large legal consequences; human reviewers should enforce absolute consistency of key terms and definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims should logically group alternative embodiments within dependent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative embodiments should be presented logically within dependent claims rather than as separate, ungrouped claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good practice groups alternatives coherently; GPT-4 was observed to perform better at grouping alternatives than some other models which listed alternatives as separate claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset and input selection constraints for evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use description-based inputs (rather than abstracts) for claim generation because descriptions contain more detailed technical/legal specifics required for claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper filters documents (e.g., granted patents filed in 2017, descriptions < 8,000 tokens) to construct the HUPD-DCG dataset. Guidance: description-based generation yields higher feature completeness and better claim outputs than abstract-based generation.
